claims.text: The degree of local chemical order controls superconducting behavior by modulating electron–phonon coupling.
Alloys with enhanced short-range order will have a higher superconducting critical temperature than fully disordered alloys of the same composition.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
Rapid quenching enforces maximal chemical disorder in the proposed alloy.
Post-synthesis annealing can promote short-range chemical order without inducing macroscopic phase separation.
The annealed and as-quenched materials should have identical overall compositions and otherwise matched processing environments.
Annealing temperature and time must be chosen to encourage local ordering while avoiding secondary-phase formation.
Short-range chemical order can be quantified using transmission electron microscopy or pair-distribution-function analysis.
Enhanced local chemical order reduces electronic impurity scattering.
Enhanced local chemical order optimizes local bonding environments.
Reduced scattering and optimized local bonding strengthen electron–phonon coupling.
Strengthened electron–phonon coupling promotes Cooper-pair formation and raises Tc.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in Tc relative to the as-quenched baseline.
The annealed alloy may exhibit a sharper superconducting transition than the as-quenched baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution and ordering does not cause macroscopic phase separation or ordered-intermetallic formation.
Normal-state resistivity measurements can be used to assess electronic scattering rates.
Failure of annealing-induced short-range order to produce a statistically significant Tc increase would falsify the central hypothesis.
An observed Tc change attributable to factors other than local chemical order would falsify the proposed causal attribution.

contradictions.description: A sharper transition is presented as optional, but the falsification rule can be read as treating failure to improve transition characteristics as falsifying. Lack of sharpening alone would not contradict the central prediction of increased Tc.
